sections.html:
• Other names: Ghost crabs
  • Scientific name: Potamocypoda pugil
  • Recommended tank size: 40 litres
  • Type: freshwater
  • Keeping: medium; breeding: difficult
  • Size: carapace up to 1 – 1.5 cm; leg span about 2.5 – 3.5 cm
  • GH: 3 – 12; KH: 1 – 5
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Lifespan: up to 3 years in captivity (2 – 3 years on average); the maximum lifespan in the wild is unknown
  • Colour: olive-brown

Potamocypoda pugil is a very small species. Distinguishing characteristics:

  • Carapace: broad, somewhat convex, smoother and more punctate on the branchial regions.
  • Colour: the carapace is olive-brown, and the limbs and underside are yellowish-brown.
  • Eyes: the orbits are short and the eyes are small and slender.
  • Legs: the walking legs are moderately slender and hairy.
  • Chelipeds: males have asymmetrical claws.

Potamocypoda parapugil is easily confused with Potamocypoda pugil because the two share many characteristics and even the same common name, Ghost crabs. In Potamocypoda parapugil, however, the chelipeds are the same shape in both males and females.
This species is endemic to Malaysia. It is found in a freshwater stream, the Sungai Kayu, in the swamp forests of eastern Johore. It is a tributary of the River Sedili.
Ghost dwarf crabs are restricted to shallow, vegetated places surrounded by shaded tropical forest.

Due to their small size, these crabs need a relatively small amount of space. A group of 4 – 6 individuals can be kept in a 20-litre tank.

If possible, a 40-litre aquarium is recommended, because larger aquariums are easier to maintain and more stable, which is important for optimal water parameters.

The tank should be cycled first. High ammonia and nitrate can harm the crabs.

Plants: these crabs are safe with any live plants. They do not eat healthy plants and can be kept in well-planted aquariums. They even benefit from live plants by cleaning microorganisms from them.

Food left uneaten should be removed after 24 hours, otherwise it fouls the water and causes problems.

• Temperature: 24 – 28°C. They do not tolerate large and sudden temperature fluctuations.
  • pH: 7.0 – 7.5
  • KH: 1 – 5
  • GH: 3 – 12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm

Water flow and aeration: these crabs enjoy water with current and rich oxygenation.

Filtration: it does not matter much and any filter can be used. For small tanks, sponge or Matten filters are the best options. These crabs are too small to damage and tear apart the sponge as large crab species often do. These filters are also cheap, easy to maintain and clean, provide lots of surface to graze on and are safe for the crabs.

Lighting: no special requirements, as the crabs are nocturnal and do not really depend on light. If there are plants, lighting should be adapted to their needs.

Decorations and hiding places: provide lots of hiding places, as they are very skittish. Decorations give shelter and protection and minimise stress, which is especially crucial during moulting, when crabs are weak and extremely vulnerable. Leaves, rocks, driftwood, PVC pipes, plastic mesh, plants and similar items can be used.

Although these crabs are fully aquatic, it is better to give them perches above the water line, for example a piece of driftwood sticking up out of the water.

Ghost dwarf crabs are omnivorous scavengers, feeding on dead or decaying plant and animal matter. This can include algae, small aquatic organisms and detritus (decomposed organic matter).

Suggested foods in aquariums:

  • blanched vegetables
  • seeds
  • algae
  • crushed snails
  • chopped blackworms, bloodworms, etc.
  • brine shrimp
  • dead fish or shrimp

They should be fed bottom-dwelling food along with sinking pellets of any brand: shrimp pellets, shrimp granules, fish food (flakes, etc.), shrimp food (crustacean food, algae wafers, etc.).

A diverse range of food is crucial for their well-being. Avoid feeding protein-rich foods continuously, even if they seem to enjoy it. Offer a combination of live food that stays at the bottom of the tank and sinking pellets from a reputable brand.

Leave the food for 24 hours before removing it. Because the crabs are mostly nocturnal, feed them at night (at least in the evening) to replicate the conditions under which they naturally eat.

Ghost dwarf crabs need permanent bodies of water, since they live in open water. Although they are fully aquatic, they can occasionally venture onto land. Although this is rare, it is recommended to give them the opportunity in the aquarium with protruding areas above the water level, such as driftwood or rocks.

They are not aggressive. Even when they dispute with one another, conflicts tend to resolve without significant harm. They are relatively shy and skittish, especially in small groups; the bigger the colony, the safer they feel and the more often they venture out of hiding. They are not very messy or destructive and are not strong enough to constantly move things in the tank.

These crabs are nocturnal. Their activity peaks from dusk and gradually stops before sunrise. This is instinctive behaviour mostly dictated by the risk of predation.

  • Social: yes
  • Activity: low
  • Peaceful: yes
  • Burrowers: no

Tankmates

Ghost dwarf crabs are among the most social and peaceful crab species. They generally bother nobody; if anything, they are more likely to receive aggression because their small size makes them a target for larger tankmates.

Fish: ideally, no aggressive, top- or middle-dwelling, fast-moving fish should be kept with them. Small, peaceful fish such as guppies, neon tetras, mollies, Danio rerio, Endlers and least killifish are examples.

Shrimp: the crabs do not hunt shrimp on purpose, but caution is advised with expensive shrimp. Shrimplets can be caught by crabs, especially when shrimp moult.

Snails: generally they do not bother freshwater snails, but very small snails may be eaten.

Bad tankmates:

  • Larger or aggressive fish
  • Bottom-dwelling, slow-moving fish and fish with long fins
  • Any crayfish species
  • Other freshwater crab species
  • Dwarf frogs

Potamocypoda pugil is sexually dimorphic.

  • Size: males are generally larger than females.
  • Abdomen: males have a narrow, slim (triangular) plate, while females have a broad plate on the belly.
  • Chelipeds: females have smaller, slender claws with spoon-shaped fingers. In males, one cheliped (right or left) is developed as in the female, and the other is greatly enlarged and modified.
  • Carapace shape: the longitudinal convexity is stronger in the female, and the anterior part of the carapace is inflated.

The reproductive traits of the genus Potamocypoda have not been described in the scientific literature. To date there are no reports of successful breeding, either in laboratory or home settings, so the duration of incubation and the number of eggs females produce are unknown.

The common name refers to their diminutive size and translucent look, which make them appear almost invisible in the tank, and to their nocturnal habit of hiding during the day. The name is also a marketing choice, since catchy names attract buyers.

Etymology: "Potamocypoda" derives from the Greek "potamos" (river) and "kupodeuein" (to walk on tiptoe), referring to the long, slender legs of these crabs.

Their rarity in the aquarium trade and the lack of scientific information on optimal care and breeding are the main problems. Given their unique appearance and small size, they can be a great addition to small aquariums.
